title: Back to School: Downstream There Is Always a Child
author: Erik Twist
summary: Erik Twist, a longtime Great Hearts Academies leader now heading Arcadia Education, lays out three first principles for school leaders opening a new year: schools exist for students, not adults; a school's culture is always downstream of its adult culture, which is downstream of its leadership culture; and love, in the 1 Corinthians 13 sense, is demanding work rather than sentiment. He warns that schools drift when staff comfort becomes the measure of institutional health, and argues that visible character-formation programs are really just the byproduct of imperfect adults publicly working at loving one another over time. Leaders, he insists, must model this personally at the headwaters rather than delegate it to protocol or rhetoric, since whatever enters the adult culture inevitably reaches a child downstream.
points: The 'headwater and stream' metaphor holds leaders accountable for culture: whatever enters at the leadership level inevitably reaches a child, so there is no dysfunction too small to matter downstream.

Twist's sharpest warning against comfort-first schools: staff satisfaction becoming the 'high-water mark of institutional health' signals a school has drifted into treating itself as a workplace first, school second.

His application of 1 Corinthians 13 to faculty rooms reframes love as documented behaviors (patience, no record of wrongs, rejoicing in truth) rather than niceness, making it a testable standard for adult culture.

Twist credits Lencioni's Five Dysfunctions of a Team not as management technique but as communal virtues underneath the business vocabulary, since vulnerability-based trust is an act of humility and healthy conflict is honesty governed by charity.
quotes: To say that the school exists for the sake of its students, that it was established to serve children, and that it is bound first to protect the promises it has made to them, is a truth with uncomfortable implications.

It shows up when a school quietly reorganizes itself around the comfort of its employees. It shows up when staff satisfaction becomes the high-water mark of institutional health, as if the school were a workplace first and a school second.
Here is the second principle: the culture of a school is always downstream of its adult culture. And the adult culture is always downstream of its leadership culture.
Downstream, there is always a child. There is no stretch of the stream that empties out somewhere harmless. Every current in the adult culture eventually reaches a kid.
Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs.
Vulnerability-based trust is an act of humility. Healthy conflict is an act of honesty governed by charity. Commitment, accountability, attention to shared results: each is love wearing work clothes.
